pages.x: In May 1618 Protestant nobles in Prague, angry that their new Catholic king, Ferdinand, was taking away their freedom of worship, threw two of his officials and a secretary out of a high castle window. All three survived: saved by angels, said Catholics; by a dung heap, said Protestants.

The Bohemians chose a Protestant king, Frederick of the Palatinate. In 1620 the Catholic armies crushed them at the White Mountain outside Prague. Frederick fled after a single winter on the throne, and was mocked ever after as the Winter King.

Albrecht von Wallenstein, a Bohemian noble grown rich on land taken from rebels, raised a vast private army for the emperor, paid for by plundering the lands it marched through. His rule was that war must feed itself.

In May 1631 imperial troops stormed the Protestant city of Magdeburg. Fire swept through it, and some 20,000 of its people were killed or burned. Germans made a new word for utter destruction: to magdeburgise.

King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Germany in 1630 to save the Protestants and win land on the Baltic. His fast, drilled army with light cannon beat the imperial armies again and again, until he was killed in the fog at Lützen in 1632.

Catholic France, led by Cardinal Richelieu, paid the Protestant Swedes, and in 1635 joined the war itself against the Catholic Habsburgs. By now it was less a war of faith than a fight for power in Europe.

Armies on every side lived off the land, looting, torturing peasants to find hidden money and spreading plague. Germany lost perhaps a fifth of its people, some regions more than half, and wolves came back to the empty villages.

Peace was made in 1648 at Münster and Osnabrück, in Westphalia, after years of talks between more than 100 delegations. Each ruler kept the right to choose his land's religion, the Dutch Republic and Switzerland were recognised as independent, and France and Sweden gained land.

The war was one of the most destructive in Europe's history. Its peace is often seen as the start of the modern system of independent states that do not meddle in each other's religion, and it left the Holy Roman Empire weak and divided for 150 years.
pts: Began with a fall from a window in Prague, 1618
Germany lost perhaps a fifth of its people
Ended by the Peace of Westphalia, 1648
